Auxiliary variables, weights and multigroup models

auxiliary.Rmd

The examples use aces (?aces): eight adverse childhood experience (ACE) items of 1,500 adults, with sex, age, parental education, a sampling weight and three adult outcomes — depressive symptoms (depress, 0–24), self-rated health (srh, 1 excellent to 5 poor) and smoking. The data were generated from four classes (Low adversity, Household dysfunction, Maltreatment, High adversity) whose membership depends on parental education and sex; the outcomes depend on the class only. The measurement model is fitted once:

library(latentmixtures)
data(aces)
m <- aces |> lca(starts_with("ace_"), K = 4)
#> Starting Julia ...
convergence(m)   # check that the best LL is replicated and EM reached the maximum
#> Convergence check: ✓ no problems found
#>   best start converged      yes (77 EM iterations)
#>   stage-2 starts converged  20 / 20
#>   best LL replicated        20 times
#>   LL at EM / after Newton   -5248.0073 / -5248.0073 (gain 5.5e-07; max |gradient| 1.6e-13)
#>   smallest class            0.099
classprobs(m)    # 1 Low adversity, 2 Maltreatment, 3 Household dysfunction, 4 High
#> [1] 0.56010632 0.18551660 0.15563172 0.09874536

Row alignment

Every auxiliary function takes the fitted model, a data frame and the columns to use: r3step(m, aces, c(female, age)), bch(m, aces, depress). The data frame must have one row per row of the data the model was fitted to, in the same order, usually the same data frame. The functions check the number of rows; they cannot check the order, so do not sort or filter the data between fitting and the auxiliary step. Rows that the model did not analyse (every indicator missing) are skipped automatically. classify(m) likewise returns one row per input row.

Covariates: one-step and three-step

Who ends up in which ACE class? One step (Mplus c ON x): with covariates, class membership is a multinomial logistic regression on the covariates, estimated jointly with the measurement model.

m1 <- aces |> lca(starts_with("ace_"), K = 4, covariates = c(female, age, low_parent_edu),
                  ref = 1)
coeftable(m1)

With Low adversity (class 1) as reference, low parental education raises the odds of every adversity class (generated log-odds +0.5 to +1.0).

Because the covariates enter the likelihood, they can change the classes themselves. Three-step estimation keeps the measurement model fixed. r3step() is Mplus AUXILIARY = x (R3STEP): the bias-adjusted three-step ML method of Vermunt (2010), which treats the most likely class as an indicator of the latent class with misclassification probabilities fixed at those of the measurement model.

r <- r3step(m, aces, c(female, age, low_parent_edu), ref = 1)
r
#> ━━ R3STEP: latent class regression (three-step) ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
#>   n = 1500; reference class 1; robust standard errors
#> 
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   Term                  Logit     SE     OR       p
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   Class 2 vs. 1
#>     (Intercept)       -0.584*  0.287  0.558   0.042

#>     low_parent_edu   0.679***  0.176  1.972  <0.001

lm_table(r, ci = TRUE, format = "markdown")

Coefficients are multinomial logits against the reference class (the last, smallest class unless ref is given), with robust standard errors (se = "ml" for ML ones). Rows with a missing covariate are deleted listwise, as in Mplus, and the number deleted is reported. Covariates must be numeric: dummy-code factors, for example with model.matrix().

Distal outcomes: BCH and DCAT

Do adults with different childhood adversity differ in their mental health today? bch() estimates the mean of a continuous distal outcome in each class with the bias-adjusted BCH method (Bolck, Croon and Hagenaars 2004; Vermunt 2010), as Mplus AUXILIARY = y (BCH), with Wald tests of equal means overall and for each pair of classes. It is robust to unequal outcome variances across classes (Bakk and Vermunt 2016). Rows with a missing outcome are excluded.

b <- bch(m, aces, depress)
b
#> ━━ BCH: distal outcome depress by class ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
#>   n = 1453 (47 rows with missing outcome excluded)
#> 
#>   ──────────────────────────────
#>   Class    Mean     SE  Variance
#>   ──────────────────────────────
#>   1       4.761  0.138    12.101
#>   2      10.259  0.297    12.933
#>   3       6.985  0.320     7.295
#>   4      13.800  0.436    12.509
#>   ──────────────────────────────
#> 
#> ── Wald tests of equal means ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────
#>   Test           Chi-square  df       p
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────
#>   Overall           647.903   3  <0.001
#>   Class 1 vs. 2     264.856   1  <0.001
#>   Class 1 vs. 3      36.417   1  <0.001
#>   Class 1 vs. 4     392.358   1  <0.001
#>   Class 2 vs. 3      51.610   1  <0.001
#>   Class 2 vs. 4      39.751   1  <0.001
#>   Class 3 vs. 4     143.693   1  <0.001
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────
b$pairwise
#>   a b     chisq            p
#> 1 1 2 264.85622 1.499728e-59
#> 2 1 3  36.41715 1.592953e-09
#> 3 1 4 392.35775 2.538616e-87
#> 4 2 3  51.61026 6.768705e-13
#> 5 2 4  39.75086 2.885141e-10
#> 6 3 4 143.69279 4.147241e-33

The generating class means of depress are 4 (Low), 9 (Maltreatment), 7 (Household) and 13 (High adversity), plus 1 for women (about half the sample). Several outcomes can be tabulated side by side; for the 0/1 smoker the BCH mean is the proportion of smokers:

lm_table(bch(m, aces, depress), bch(m, aces, smoker), pairwise = TRUE, format = "markdown")

dcat() handles a categorical distal outcome by the method of Lanza, Tan and Bray (2013), as Mplus AUXILIARY = y (DCAT). It returns the outcome distribution in each class, its standard errors, odds ratios (each category against the first, relative to class ref) and Wald tests. Self-rated health:

srh <- factor(aces$srh, 1:5, c("excellent", "very good", "good", "fair", "poor"))
aces_f <- transform(aces, srh = srh)
dc <- dcat(m, aces_f, srh, ref = 1)
round(dc$probs, 3)    # fair and poor health are most common in the High adversity class
#>            1     2     3     4     5
#> class1 0.245 0.395 0.254 0.079 0.026
#> class2 0.171 0.294 0.314 0.147 0.074
#> class3 0.164 0.346 0.302 0.164 0.024
#> class4 0.093 0.288 0.319 0.240 0.060
dc$oddsratio
#>        1        2        3        4        5
#> class1 1 1.000000 1.000000 1.000000 1.000000
#> class2 1 1.065471 1.771165 2.652593 4.105217
#> class3 1 1.309725 1.771768 3.094911 1.393554
#> class4 1 1.927803 3.318925 7.998063 6.142484
lm_table(dc, format = "html")

The outcome may be a factor, character or numeric codes; factor labels are kept.

Sampling weights

The sample over-represents adults whose parents had no post-secondary education (45% against 30% in the population); weight undoes this. weights takes a column of the data (or a numeric vector). As in Mplus, weights are rescaled to sum to the number of analysed rows; the log-likelihood, parameters, class proportions and robust standard errors are weighted, and r3step() and bch() use the model’s weights.

mw <- aces |> lca(starts_with("ace_"), K = 4, weights = weight)
rbind(unweighted = classprobs(m), weighted = classprobs(mw))   # fewer high-adversity adults
#>                 [,1]      [,2]      [,3]       [,4]
#> unweighted 0.5601063 0.1855166 0.1556317 0.09874536
#> weighted   0.5886255 0.1780398 0.1455871 0.08774761
bch(mw, aces, depress)
#> ━━ BCH: distal outcome depress by class ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
#>   n = 1453 (47 rows with missing outcome excluded)
#> 
#>   ──────────────────────────────
#>   Class    Mean     SE  Variance
#>   ──────────────────────────────
#>   1       4.787  0.143    12.017
#>   2      10.310  0.308    12.881
#>   3       6.984  0.341     6.973
#>   4      14.059  0.486    12.830
#>   ──────────────────────────────
#> 
#> ── Wald tests of equal means ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────
#>   Test           Chi-square  df       p
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────
#>   Overall           583.160   3  <0.001
#>   Class 1 vs. 2     250.256   1  <0.001
#>   Class 1 vs. 3      31.700   1  <0.001
#>   Class 1 vs. 4     336.847   1  <0.001
#>   Class 2 vs. 3      48.622   1  <0.001
#>   Class 2 vs. 4      37.838   1  <0.001
#>   Class 3 vs. 4     127.929   1  <0.001
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────

Weighting moves the class shares towards the population, in which low parental education and hence childhood adversity are less common (generated population shares 0.55, 0.19, 0.16, 0.10 for Low, Household dysfunction, Maltreatment, High adversity). The bootstrap LRT (blrt()) is not available with weights; lmr() is not available with covariates.

Multigroup models and measurement invariance

Do women and men report childhood adversity in the same way? With group (Mplus KNOWNCLASS), class proportions differ across known groups and invariance sets the measurement model (Clogg and Goodman 1985):

  • "full": the item-response probabilities are equal across groups (measurement invariance), so classes mean the same in every group and their sizes can be compared;
  • "none": every group has its own measurement model;
  • a vector of indicator names: those items are group-specific (partial invariance).

In the generating model sexual abuse (ace_sex_abuse) is more often reported by women in every class, and all other items are invariant.

full <- aces |> lca(starts_with("ace_"), K = 4, group = female)
part <- aces |> lca(starts_with("ace_"), K = 4, group = female, invariance = "ace_sex_abuse")
none <- aces |> lca(starts_with("ace_"), K = 4, group = female, invariance = "none")
convergence(part)
#> Convergence check: ✓ no problems found
#>   best start converged      yes (84 EM iterations)
#>   stage-2 starts converged  20 / 20
#>   best LL replicated        20 times
#>   LL at EM / after Newton   -6263.9010 / -6263.9010 (gain 6.7e-07; max |gradient| 9.7e-14)
#>   smallest class            0.096
classprobs(full)                          # class-by-group proportions (men, women)
#>            [,1]      [,2]
#> [1,] 0.54743158 0.5670998
#> [2,] 0.17552235 0.1928102
#> [3,] 0.18346359 0.1341350
#> [4,] 0.09358248 0.1059550
itemprobs(part, group = 2)$ace_sex_abuse  # women
#>       class1    class2     class3    class4
#> 0 0.92670967 0.5233015 0.91077561 0.3959592
#> 1 0.07329033 0.4766985 0.08922439 0.6040408
itemprobs(part, group = 1)$ace_sex_abuse  # men
#>      class1    class2     class3    class4
#> 0 0.9859012 0.7820709 0.93668586 0.6338656
#> 1 0.0140988 0.2179291 0.06331414 0.3661344

Groups are numbered in the order of levels(factor(female)) (0 = men, 1 = women). The invariance models are nested with the same number of classes, so compare_models() tests them with the Satorra-Bentler scaled difference test that Mplus uses under MLR, alongside the naive likelihood-ratio test and the differences in AIC and BIC:

compare_models(full, part)                # freeing ace_sex_abuse improves the fit
#> ━━ Nested model comparison ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
#>   full (M0) nested in part (M1)
#> 
#>   ──────────────────────────────────
#>   Model            LL  Par.  Scaling
#>   ──────────────────────────────────
#>   M0: full  -6285.709    39   1.0374
#>   M1: part  -6263.901    43   1.0381
#>   ──────────────────────────────────
#> 
#> ── Difference tests ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   Test                          Chi-square  df       p
#>   ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   Likelihood ratio (naive, ML)      43.615   4  <0.001
#>   Satorra-Bentler scaled (MLR)      41.724   4  <0.001
#>   ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   Scaling correction of the difference cd = 1.0453
#>   ΔAIC = -35.615, ΔBIC = -14.362, ΔsaBIC = -27.069 (M1 - M0)
cmp <- compare_models(full, part, none)   # each model against the previous one
cmp
#> Nested model comparison
#> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Model  K  Par.         LL  Scaling        BIC  df  Chi-square      cd  Scaled chi-square  Scaled p
#> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> full   4    39  -6285.709   1.0374  12856.633   —           —       —                  —         —
#> part   4    43  -6263.901   1.0381  12842.271   4      43.615  1.0453             41.724    <0.001
#> none   4    71  -6248.025   1.0573  13015.290  28      31.751  1.0868             29.215     0.402
#> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Each model is tested against the previous one. Scaling = MLR scaling correction factor; cd = scaling correction of the difference; scaled test = Satorra-Bentler (Mplus MLR).
lm_table(cmp, format = "markdown")

full 4 39 -6285.709 1.0374 12856.633 — — — — —
part 4 43 -6263.901 1.0381 12842.271 4 43.615 1.0453 41.724 <0.001

Each model is tested against the previous one. Scaling = MLR scaling correction factor; cd = scaling correction of the difference; scaled test = Satorra-Bentler (Mplus MLR).

Partial invariance is preferred over full invariance, and freeing the other seven items as well ("none") does not improve the fit further — the generating model.

lpa() takes group and invariance in the same way.

With covariates, the class logits of a multigroup model have group-specific intercepts and covariate slopes equal across groups (slopes = "equal", Mplus c ON cg; c ON x) or group-specific (slopes = "group"); weights work as in a single-group model:

mgc <- aces |> lca(starts_with("ace_"), K = 4, group = female, invariance = "ace_sex_abuse",
                   covariates = low_parent_edu, slopes = "group", weights = weight)
coeftable(mgc)           # intercepts by group, low_parent_edu slopes by group
#>           kind group class           item        level    estimate         se

Direct effects of covariates on indicators (DIF)

The multigroup model treats sex as a grouping variable. A one-group alternative keeps sex as a covariate of the classes and adds a direct effect of sex on the sexual-abuse item — differential item functioning (Mplus u ON x; Masyn 2017): within every class, women report it with higher odds than men.

dif <- aces |> lca(starts_with("ace_"), K = 4, covariates = c(female, low_parent_edu),
                   direct = list(ace_sex_abuse = female))
dif                       # "Direct effects" block: ace_sex_abuse ON female

pt[pt$kind == "direct effect", c("class", "item", "level", "estimate", "se", "p")]
#>    class          item  level estimate        se            p
#> 14     1 ace_sex_abuse female 1.128459 0.1843998 9.379036e-10

The slope is equal across classes by default (u ON x in %OVERALL%); list the item in classspecific for class-specific slopes. Continuous indicators work the same way in lpa(..., direct = list(y = x)).

Local dependence

Latent class models assume that the items are independent within class. bvr() gives the bivariate residual of every pair of categorical indicators (Pearson chi-square of the observed against the model-implied two-way table, divided by its df; Mplus TECH10):

m3 <- aces |> lca(starts_with("ace_"), K = 3)
head(bvr(m3))             # BVR above about 3.84 suggests local dependence
#> Bivariate residuals (Pearson chi-square / df; > 3.84 suggests local dependence)
#> 
#>           item1            item2 pearson    lr df   bvr
#>  ace_phys_abuse  ace_emo_neglect   8.767 8.958  1 8.767
#>   ace_emo_abuse    ace_sex_abuse   4.106 4.073  1 4.106
#>   ace_emo_abuse ace_phys_neglect   4.079 4.154  1 4.079
#>  ace_phys_abuse    ace_sex_abuse   3.290 3.221  1 3.290
#>   ace_sex_abuse ace_phys_neglect   3.206 3.097  1 3.206
#>   ace_emo_abuse   ace_phys_abuse   3.134 3.163  1 3.134

A pair with a large BVR can be modelled jointly with a within-class log-linear association (Hagenaars 1988), class-specific (association = "varying", the pair as one joint item) or equal across classes:

b <- bvr(m3)
ld <- aces |> lca(starts_with("ace_"), K = 3, pairs = c(b$item1[1], b$item2[1]),
                  association = "equal")
c(independent = BIC(m3), dependent_pair = BIC(ld))
#>    independent dependent_pair 
#>       10822.45       10810.04

For continuous indicators, lpa(..., with = list(c(y1, y2))) frees selected within-class covariances (Mplus y1 WITH y2).
